I'm Aiko. I'll be next to you the whole time, and I'll say something when it matters. There are three things to try in here, and none of them are a test.

Three to play · more on the way

Lumisphere

A place to work out how the internet actually tries to get you, by being the one who has to stop it. Guard an inbox at 2am. Read somebody's posts the way a stranger would. Hold a vault shut while a machine tries every password there is. Aiko is with you the whole way.

Game four locked Is This Real? A photo that never happened, a video of somebody who does not exist. Work out what is actually in front of you. Fakes and AI pictures · coming soon
Game five locked Who Can See This? Every app asks for something. Find out who is really on the other side of a setting you never changed. Privacy and permissions · coming soon
Game six locked Free Stuff, Real Money Skins, coins, a deal that ends in ten minutes. Spot the ones that quietly want a real card number. Money traps in games · coming soon

Best on a big screen. All three work with touch.

What you've learned so far, 0 of 11
For grown-ups, what these actually teach

Night Shift is about messages other people send. It drills one habit: judge a message by what it asks you to do, not by whether it looks scary. Several "safe" messages deliberately contain alarming words so that blocking on vibes alone loses points.

Breadcrumbs is about what a child publishes themselves. They play the stranger first, assembling a real-world picture out of six ordinary posts, and only then go back and fix it. Deleting everything is scored as a loss, because "post nothing" is advice no child follows.

Vault is about the account itself. A child builds passwords from parts and watches a cracking machine attack them, so the lesson arrives as a number rather than a rule: four random words hold for a thousand years, while a dictionary word with a digit and a symbol on the end falls in under a second. The cracker is deliberately seeded with the facts leaked in Breadcrumbs, the pet, the street, the birthday , so "unusual to me" and "hard to guess" come apart. It ends on password reuse, which is the failure most adults have too.

Between them the games cover nine common tricks, the footprint problem and account security. Two things are treated as different in kind from the rest, and it is worth knowing why:

  • Secrecy, anyone asking a child to hide a conversation from you.
  • Moving somewhere private, a push into DMs, another app, photos or camera.

For those two, the game will not let a child "win" by blocking and moving on. It makes them press a second button to fetch an adult, because handling it alone is the wrong lesson. The single most useful thing you can say afterwards is that they will never be in trouble for showing you something. Children stay quiet because they expect to lose the tablet, not because they didn't spot it.
